https://www.politico.eu/article/afd-far-.text: Five years ago, the Alternative for Germany’s campaign posters in Saxony-Anhalt carried a single bleak word: “Enough.” This month, the far-right party won a historic landslide in the eastern German state by offering something different: “Everything is Possible.” Arguably, it was an AfD version of Barack Obama’s 2008 rallying cry: “Yes We Can.” That change — from grumbling exasperation to upbeat optimism — helps explain why the AfD has surged at the ballot box, putting its first state government within reach earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt and setting it up to hit historic highs in two further state elections on Sunday, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Advertisement Advertisement Others have taken note, and it might well serve as a new campaigning template for far-right populists across Europe — at least for those able to flash a credible smile. “I call it feel-good populism,” said Johannes Hillje, a Berlin-based political consultant who managed the European Green Party’s 2014 European Parliament campaign. “What we saw was a new type of AfD campaign.” “In the past it has been mainly negative rhetoric, scapegoating migrants, attacking the elite, evoking fear and rage,” Hillje added. “If you really want to mobilize people, it’s not enough just to attack others. You also have to offer a positive perspective.” At its core, the AfD continues to hold a dark vision of Germany’s path — depicting the country as on the brink of catastrophe due to the destructive forces of migration and deindustrialization. The party’s intellectual ideologues espouse an almost apocalyptic view of the decline of Germany and the West. Yet in recent elections, the party has papered over this ideological core with a cheerful, reassuring facade, seeking to marry hope with fear. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund was labeled by one magazine “Germany’s most dangerous man.” But at campaign stops and in television appearances, he projected another image: He kept an almost permanent smile on his face, was invariably polite and friendly, took selfies with voters and rode his sky-blue vintage East German-era scooter. Advertisement Advertisement Siegmund combined the forward-looking “Everything is Possible” with another slogan, “Bring Back the Good Old Times,” fusing nostalgia and hope, a powerful combination for people worried about the rapid pace of disruptive change and an uncertain future. “He’s become a bit of a pop star, and that explains a lot about why the AfD doubled its vote,” said the German-British historian Katja Hoyer. “It also helps explain why there was a smaller gap between men and women in Saxony-Anhalt. In the national vote, far more men than women vote for the AfD.” Hoyer believes the appeal won’t be confined to Germany. Others will learn from it. Alice Weidel, Ulrich Siegmund and Tino Chrupalla celebrate following state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, 2026. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images In the summer of 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declared that “the center is holding.” Following that year’s European Parliament elections, it seemed voters still largely backed centrist parties, despite significant gains by right-wing populists and national conservatives. But a succession of elections since then, including Saxony-Anhalt, has suggested that Europe may be further from peak populism than many centrists hoped. Marco Tarchi, an Italian political scientist at the University of Florence, believes populism in Europe still has further to go. “Political narratives rather than policy details drive voter behavior,” he told POLITICO. For right-wing populists, he said, it will be crucial to ensure that their narratives focus on the issues potential voters deem most important. Hoyer’s latest book, “ Weimar ,” chronicles interwar Germany and the rise of the Nazis through Weimar, the birthplace of the country’s first full democracy. She has closely observed this month’s state elections and, while dismissing comparisons with the late 1920s, acknowledged some parallels. Advertisement Advertisement “There’s certainly something in the air that causes lots of politicians to refer to Weimar and to the Nazi era,” she said. But she cautioned that the periods were very different, particularly when it came to political violence. “Whatever the similarities, we don’t see the AfD running around with armed people on the streets intimidating and murdering opponents,” she added. But Hoyer sees one important echo: Voters worried about the future are looking to parties that offer a clearer vision than moderates. After the Wall Street crash, Germans got austerity from Chancellor Heinrich Brüning. Hitler, by contrast, promised: “Give me four years, and I will sort it all out,” she said. “I fear there’s a similarity now,” she added. “People don’t see solutions coming from the mainstream parties, who point to geopolitics and say, ‘What can we do?’ Meanwhile, the AfD and some other right-wing populists say, ‘We will do X, Y, and Z.’” “It doesn’t even have to be realistic,” she said. “I think people just want to feel that somebody has got some sort of plan.”

https://www.ksl.com:443/article/51624675.text: TALLINN, Estonia — The U.S. special envoy for Belarus said Wednesday that the country's authorities have agreed to release 25 prisoners in exchange for the lifting of U.S. sanctions against two Belarusian companies.John Coale, President Donald Trump's special envoy for Belarus, made the statement a day after meeting Belarus' authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko, who pushed for the remaining U.S. sanctions against his country to be lifted."25 prisoners are free today!" Coale said on X, adding that "President Trump's commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results." He also thanked Lukashenko and authorities in Lithuania, a European Union member that neighbors Belarus, for their support."We will continue to improve U.S.-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future," Coale said. "We are not finished!"Speaking to reporters in Minsk, Coale said as part of what he called "an interim deal" and "as a show of good will," Belarus will release 25 people in exchange for the U.S. lifting sanctions on two Belarusian companies, Lakokraska and Bellesbumprom.He added that further release of prisoners and the lifting of more sanctions will follow later after all details are agreed upon.Belarusian authorities haven't announced any details of the prisoners' release yet.Lukashenko has governed the nation of 9.5 million with an iron fist for more than three decades, and the country has been sanctioned repeatedly by Western countries — both for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing Moscow to use its territory to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Since Trump returned to the White House for his second term, Lukashenko has released hundreds of political prisoners in a series of U.S.-mediated deals that also lifted some U.S. sanctions.Belarusian opposition leader-in-exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya welcomed the prisoners' release, but noted that many others remain in custody."This is an important step, but only a step," Tsikhanouskaya told The Associated Press. https://euobserver.com/244873/czech-gove.text: First published in Deník N. The lower house of Czech parliament became a nighttime battleground for the future of the country’s public service media at the weekend, when MPs pushed through the abolition of public service media licence fees in the bill’s first reading in the chamber on Saturday (24 October). Czech MPs voted to pass a bill that lays the groundwork to abolish TV and radio licence fees and move public media under the state budget. The weekend vote was not yet a vote on the law’s final approval: the government coalition only needed to prevent the bill’s rejection which the opposition had sought. The controversial vote was scheduled for 4.36am on Saturday – by no means a typical time for such a vote. Opposition parties had failed to postpone the vote, and also did not have enough numbers to reject the bill. Out of 177 lawmakers present, 96 MPs voted in favour of the bill, while 81 opposition MPs voted to reject it. Prime minister Andrej Babiš did not take part in the vote. MPs from the Czech Republic’s five opposition parties also failed to pass a proposal to return the bill for redrafting to the coalition formed by ANO (led by the PM) and the far-right parties Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) and Motorists to Themselves. The bill will now go to the parliament's media and culture committee. This will be followed by lengthy debate at the law's second reading, where amendments may be submitted. The proceedings will likely last several days. Read more PM Babiš blames press for ANO election loss, renews calls to abolish license fees for Czech public media 4.36am vote planned at last-minute Babiš’s governing majority only added the agenda item for ending licence fees on the Chamber of Deputies’ (lower house of parliament's) agenda on Friday morning. It even took by surprise the MPs of ANO, SPD and Motorists. The coalition leadership formed by Babiš and foreign minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) had kept the plan secret all week, so that it would not become public and opposition parties could not prepare obstruction tactics. Protesters had gathered outside the parliament through the night in the early hours of Saturday morning. Demonstrations carried on throughout the Czech Republic over the weekend.
